Skip next section Right-wing commentator arrested over sexual assault remarks targeting protesters 08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 Right-wing commentator arrested over sexual assault remarks targeting protesters Right-wing accounts on social media are targeting the women at the CJP protests, reports say [FILE: July 25, 2026] Image: Sajjad Hussain/AFP An activist who considers himself a right-wing "political commentator" was arrested in the southern state of Kerala on Sunday over remarks he allegedly made about the women at the Cockroach Janta Party-led student protests last month, media reports said. The case was registered following a complaint alleging that videos on TG Mohandas' YouTube channel, Pathrika, were intended to disturb public order and create fear and unrest . According to reports, in the videos, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi protests could lead to gang rape and claimed that women attending it "like rape" and that some "enjoy being raped." He also called for police to open fire at protesters. News channel NDTV reported that Mohandas is a former member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). However, the RSS has denied any association with the commentator. The BJP on Monday criticized the arrest as "discriminatory" and accused the Kerala government of attempting to divert attention from other issues, reports said. Women protesters being targeted online The development comes amid an online campaign targeting women who took part in CJP-led student protests. The countrywide stir ended last month with the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Multiple reports indicate that young women involved in the movement are facing severe online harassment . They have been targeted with fake and AI-manipulated images, as well as a barrage of online abuse, including assault threats. Read more A Nato F-18 fighter jet operating on an air policing mission has shot down a drone that unlawfully entered Romanian airspace, marking the fourth unmanned craft brought down over the country this year, Romania 's defence ministry announced on Sunday. The aircraft was initially detected by radar as it crossed into Romanian territory from neighbouring Moldova, 24 km north of the south-eastern city of Galati. Although Romania's defence ministry did not specify the drone's origin, Nato representatives suggested a Russian link. A spokesperson for Nato military headquarters, U.S. Army Colonel Martin O'Donnell, reaffirmed that the alliance is constantly monitoring threats and stands ready to act. He said: "Additional details regarding Sunday’s incident remain under investigation, but the drone appears to be Russian." Romania, a Nato member with a 614 km (381 miles) land border with Ukraine, has recorded numerous airspace incursions by Russian drones over the last four years, alongside floating sea mines threatening key Black Sea shipping and energy routes. In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace for the first time after dozens of such incursions since the start of Russia's war in Ukraine ( AFP/Getty ) The F-18 jet, part of a Spanish Nato contingent deployed in Romania, "made radar contact with the target and received permission to engage", the ministry said in a statement, adding that the drone was shot down safely at 5.01am (0201 GMT). The ministry said that fragments from the destroyed drone appeared to have fallen in an uninhabited area between two villages. In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace for the first time after dozens of such incursions since the start of Russia 's war in Ukraine. In May, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment block in Galati during an overnight attack on neighbouring Ukraine, injuring two people. https://www.mirror.co.uk/tv/tv-news/who-.text: The Netflix series links characters based on historical figures with the infamous tale. Now in its fourth instalment since its original debut back in 2022, the true crime-inspired series Monster has returned to retell another high-profile case. This time around, it is of Lizzie Borden . *Warning - this article contains mild spoilers for Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story* While the series focuses on Borden, it also spends a lot of time telling the apparent story of Elizabeth Bathory. But who was she really? What do history experts say, and how is she portrayed in Netflix's Monster? Here's all you need to know. Elizabeth Bathory was a noblewoman in Hungary who lived from 1560 to 1614. She came from a powerful family that owned land in the then Kingdom of Hungary. She was accused, along with four of her servants, of torturing and killing hundreds of girls between 1590 and 1614. Some scholars claim that these accusations were supported by as many as 300 people. However, it has also been suggested that these accusations were made solely to destroy the Bathory family's influence and standing. Bathory and the others were eventually charged with 80 counts of murder and convicted. At her trial, key witnesses who worked where she lived claimed to see some horrendous acts. Bathory's servants were all executed following conviction, but she was imprisoned in the Castle of Csejte (in Slovakia) until her death. Her alleged crimes sparked many rumours and wild stories both before her arrest and especially in the years afterward. She became the subject of local folklore, and one of the most common tales shared was that she bathed in her victims' blood to retain beauty and or her youth. However, despite horrific witness accounts and claims, none of them mentioned this. Nevertheless, she soon became often referenced as the Blood Countess. That is how Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story portrays her. In fact, much like how it treats Lizzie herself, the show takes the stance that Bathory is definitely guilty of her crimes, a monster herself, and also some kind of inspiration for Borden. This is reflected in the fact that Vicky Krieps plays the role, while she also appears as the Borden family maid and is portrayed as Lizzie's accomplice, despite there being no evidence of it actually happening. More recently, University of Cambridge associate professor Dr Annouchka Bayley has suggested what really happened. In 2024, she put forward that Bathory's victims may have actually been girls she helped and assisted in being smuggled elsewhere, which explains their disappearance. Dr Bayley told the BBC : "Who has the time in one lifetime to, one by one, kill 650 young women? I mean, she would have been a busy girl. I dug, and I dug, and all of those 650 women belonged to one particular class of young women who were basically the people who lived in that region before the Hungarians came. "You've got a bunch of unmarriageable teenage deposed noblewomen. So what Bathory did was set up a school to teach them how to read and offered them sanctuary." Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is streaming on Netflix.
